newsitem.title: GERMANY: German commentators sceptical about "tax summit".
newsitem.headline: German commentators sceptical about "tax summit".

text.p: German commentators on Tuesday welcomed the first meeting of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) over tax reforms but were sceptical about an early deal.

Kohl's centre-right coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU) and Free Democrats (FDP) met on Monday with SPD party chairman Oskar Lafontaine and other leading SPD officials to seek a compromise tax reform in a bid to fight record unemployment.
Government and opposition officials came away from that meeting saying there had been little progress on substantial issues, but that they would meet again on Friday.
The government is proposing to cut income tax rates and thereby lower taxes as much as 30 billion marks ($18 billion).

Germany's most widely-read newspaper, the mass daily Bild, urged politicians to "Hurry Up!" in an editorial, saying the good news was that the two sides had "finally begun to try to find a common solution for tax reform."
"German politics have become too slow -- a system of complacency," Bild wrote.

In a reference to the government's plans to raise taxes on night work, overtime and holiday work, the paper said: "Of course, Bonn (politicians) like to talk about overtime and night work, but they do this too infrequently themselves."
The daily Die Welt was "deeply sceptical" that the two sides could agree on a quick compromise and questioned whether the SPD was serious about working together with the government on tax reform.
"The fate of 4.7 million unemployed must be an imperative for the SPD," Welt wrote. "If Lafontaine really wants to help them, then he must make compromises."
"No Closer After First Meeting Over Tax Reform," said the conservative daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung in its main story.

And the liberal Frankfurter Rundschau said the nearly three-hour meeting gave no indication of which direction future "tax summits" would take and called the government's goal of halving unemployment by 2000 just "Waiting for Godot".
There were also a few less sceptical commentators, who considered the fact that government and opposition were sitting down together at all as a step in the right direction.

"Damned to Succeed" said the Bonn daily General-Anzeiger, adding: "The coalition and the SPD have cleared perhaps the most difficult hurdle. They are sitting together again at the table in order to resolve the most urgent problems together."
Germany's leading economic daily, Handelblatt, was also optimistic that the talks had already produced a modest amount of consensus on cutting tax burdens for companies in 1998.
"The tax reform has more to do with strengthening the economy in 1998 and less with tax rates on individuals," it said. ($ = 1.677 German Marks)
